I've got an acre that is irrigated by flood irrigation, but have been working to convert that to zones to better suit the crops I am growing. Originally I put in a bunch of 1/2 inch schedule 40 as a stop gap, with multiple small zones that are manually managed. These are fed off a pump, but as I'm at work all day when the irrigation runs, it became too much for my wife to manage with 60 plus zones. That, and the pump put out too much psi and blew out a bunch of pipe.

I'm working on doing a run of 1.5 inch schedule 40 as a main, with 1 inch for each zone. Each 3.5 gpm impact sprinkler will run off one dedicated 1/2 inch pipe off of the 1 inch, with no more than 4 sprinklers per zone.

The 1.5 is rated at about 450 psi, and the 1 inch at about 350 psi. My thinking is that I can get away with an 800 psi pump and run two zones at a time, for a total of 8 impact sprinklers at 28 gpm. All zones will still be manually managed, but going with wide area impact sprinklers over small rotary sprinklers drastically cuts down on the number of zones to manage.

I'm just worried I'm going overkill with a 1.5 inch main, and wanted to get a second opinion before I drop a butt load of cash on piping.
Who knows enough about irrigation to tell me if I'm doing this right?

Have a degree in chemical engineering, but unfortunately don't know that much about designing an irrigation system. In an attempt to not be completely unhelpful, I found you a video with some advice that might be of use. https://youtube.com/watch?v=DWV-pnt9EJw

From what I see on the jobs that I manage, your main line seems too small, with too few sprinklers on each zone, and your pressure is too high unless your pumping up a significant grade.

You need volume, not necessarily pressure to achieve flow with irrigation, so back off the pressure and upgrade the diameter of your main line. Then look into getting a controller for $1500 or so. Most commercial controllers can handle 30 to 50 zones.

How many acres are you trying to cover?

Really appreciate the input.

Pressure is unfortunately a side effect of the pump, and I can't change that out right now. The pump has to be primed, and in the time it takes to prime it and then switch on a zone, it will build up to max pressure.

The reason I went with 1.5 is because that is the impeller intake size on the pump, and I was worried that increasing the diameter on the output side would drop the pressure and not allow the sprinklers to cover their area. I just don't know where to begin with calculations on that. I've mostly been going with gpm of the pipe and dividing it down with each step down to the different zones.

I'm only covering an acre with this, but the number of sprinklers per zone has to remain small. It's an ornamental landscape done with a large amount of berry bushes and fruit trees, so each zone controls the water rate to specific plant types. My planned layout is 16 zones, so much more easily managed than the massive number of .25 drip, rotor, and soaker lines I originally put in. Those actually worked great when I was running it off of house water, but the deposits in the water from the irrigation ditch fouled them up immediately when I hooked it up to the pump.

What I'm working with is a ditch that run from the mountains, diverts a portion to each shareholder, and flows into a 30k gallon pond I dug. I get enough water to fill that pond in an hour, then pump out of it.
The pressures your pushing are way too high. What are you growing and is the soil that high drainage?

The pressure is what the pump is capable of producing directly at the output in between priming it and turning on the first zone. I can get a regulator for it, but I can only reduce it so much.

I'm growing virtually everything. Each zone is for a specific plant type, ie mature trees, fruit trees, fruit bushes, annual food crops, etc. It is done as an ornamental landscape though, so it's not row crops.

The soil is high drainage, but I have virtually unlimited water. Any over watering quickly makes its way back into the river.
